chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl bin Ziyad and Ali bin Ibrahim from his father, all from Ibn Fazzal, from Saeed bin Muhammad al-Tahiri, from his father, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), who said:
A man asked him about the selling of the singing slave-girls, so he said: 'Buying them and selling them is prohibited, and teaching them is disbelief, and listening to them is hypocrisy.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on buying, selling, and listening to female singing slave-girls in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes a tripartite legal and spiritual framework regarding female singing slave-girls, categorizing their trade as prohibited, their training as disbelief, and listening to them as hypocrisy. In Shia jurisprudence, this serves as a primary evidence for the impermissibility of entertainment that distracts from spiritual devotion, linking the physical act of commerce with the internal state of the believer's heart. The progression from haram to kufr to nifaq highlights the escalating spiritual consequences of engaging with this specific form of artistic performance.
